nodes.label: Thutmose III
nodes.full: Thutmose III, who ruled alone from about 1458 after the regency of Hatshepsut, led seventeen campaigns in Syria and Palestine, took Megiddo, reached the Euphrates and made Egypt for the first time the ruler of a Levantine empire, with garrisons and tribute from Syria and Nubia; the annals at Karnak record his campaigns and the booty of his reign.
nodes.src: Thutmose III, Annals at Karnak; Donald Redford, The Wars in Syria and Palestine of Thutmose III (2003); Marc Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016).

nodes.label: Amenhotep III
nodes.full: Amenhotep III ruled in an age of peace with the other Great Kings, maintained by diplomatic marriages and letters, and built on a vast scale at Thebes, with the temple of Luxor, the mortuary temple with the Colossi of Memnon and the palace of Malkata; the Amarna letters, found at his son's capital, show his correspondence with Mitanni, Babylon, Hatti, Assyria and Alashiya.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters (EA 1–30; trans. William Moran, 1992); Arielle Kozloff, Amenhotep III (2012); Eric Cline and David O'Connor (eds.), Amenhotep III: Perspectives on His Reign (2012).

nodes.label: Akhenaten and Nefertiti
nodes.full: Amenhotep IV took the name Akhenaten, promoted the sole worship of the sun-disc Aten, built a new city at Akhetaten (Amarna) in Middle Egypt and neglected the empire's Syrian vassals, whose appeals for help fill the Amarna letters; after his death the court returned to Thebes under Tutankhamun and, in the next generation under Horemheb, his name was erased from the records.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters; Barry Kemp, The City of Akhenaten and Nefertiti (2012); Aidan Dodson, Amarna Sunset (2009).

nodes.label: Ramesses II
nodes.full: Ramesses II, who ruled for 66 years from his residence at Pi-Ramesses in the Delta, fought the Hittites at Qadesh in his fifth year, concluded a treaty with Hattusili III in his twenty-first, married a Hittite princess and covered Egypt and Nubia with monuments, among them Abu Simbel and the Ramesseum; he outlived twelve of his sons.
nodes.src: Kenneth Kitchen, Pharaoh Triumphant (1982); Ramesses II inscriptions at Abu Simbel; Van De Mieroop 2016.

nodes.label: Mitanni
nodes.full: The Hurrian kingdom of Mitanni, with its capital Washukanni on the Khabur, dominated northern Mesopotamia and Syria from about 1500, with kings such as Saushtatar, who took the doors of the palace of Assur; Artatama, Shuttarna II and Tushratta, who gave his daughter Tadukhepa to Amenhotep III, were the Great Kings of the Amarna letters, until Tushratta was murdered and the kingdom was shattered by Hatti and Assyria.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters EA 17–29; Nuzi tablets; Trevor Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (1998).

nodes.label: Suppiluliuma I
nodes.full: Suppiluliuma I, the greatest of the Hittite kings, rebuilt Hattusa, destroyed Mitanni's power in the One-Year War, took Syria, set up his sons as viceroys at Carchemish and Aleppo and received the request of an Egyptian queen, perhaps Ankhesenamun, to send her a son to marry; the prince died on the way, and the Hittite army brought home a plague that killed the king.
nodes.src: Deeds of Suppiluliuma (ed. Güterbock, 1956); Bryce 1998; Itamar Singer, Hittite Prayers (2002).

nodes.label: Muwatalli II and Hattusili III
nodes.full: Muwatalli II moved the capital to Tarhuntassa in the south, fought Ramesses at Qadesh and held Syria; his brother Hattusili III took the throne from his nephew Urhi-Teshub, in a civil war that left a weaker kingdom, and ruled with his wife Puduhepa, who corresponded with Ramesses and the Kassite king, and made peace with Egypt in 1259 BC.
nodes.src: Apology of Hattusili III; Bryce 1998; Trevor Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005).

nodes.label: Kassite Babylon
nodes.full: The Kassite dynasty of Babylon, which had replaced the house of Hammurabi about 1595, ruled for four centuries with kings like Kurigalzu I, who built Dur-Kurigalzu, Burnaburiash II, who corresponded with Amenhotep and Akhenaten as a brother and equal, and Kadashman-Enlil I, a period of peace and great scribal activity in which Akkadian became the language of diplomacy.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters EA 1–14; Babylonian King List A; John Brinkman, A Political History of Post-Kassite Babylonia (1968).

nodes.label: Ashur-uballit I and Assyria
nodes.full: Ashur-uballit, who took advantage of the fall of Mitanni to make Assyria independent, wrote to Akhenaten as a Great King and a brother, which the Babylonian Burnaburiash protested, and gave his daughter in marriage to the Kassite king; his successors Adad-nirari I and Shalmaneser I took the Mitannian lands to the Euphrates and Tukulti-Ninurta I took Babylon about 1225.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters EA 15–16; Assyrian King List; A. Kirk Grayson, Assyrian Royal Inscriptions vol. 1 (1972).

nodes.label: Vassals of Canaan and Syria
nodes.full: The rulers of Byblos, Tyre, Jerusalem, Shechem and Megiddo, among them Rib-Hadda of Byblos, Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem and Labayu of Shechem, wrote to the pharaoh in Akkadian more than 300 letters preserved at Amarna, complaining of each other, begging for troops and protesting loyalty; the letters show a world of small city-states under an Egyptian overlordship, in conflict with the habiru and the Amorite kings of the north.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters EA 68–155, 227–290; Nadav Na'aman, Canaan in the Second Millennium BCE (2005); Moran 1992.

nodes.label: Ugarit
nodes.full: The kingdom of Ugarit on the Syrian coast, a vassal of Egypt and then of Hatti, with kings such as Niqmaddu II, Ammistamru II and Ammurapi, was a trading city of some 6,000 people that held the archive of its palace in several languages, among them the local alphabetic cuneiform, and was destroyed about 1185 BC; its tablets are the main source for a vassal state of the age.
nodes.src: Ugarit tablets (KTU); Marguerite Yon, The City of Ugarit at Tell Ras Shamra (2006); Mark Smith, The Ugaritic Baal Cycle (1994).

nodes.label: Megiddo
nodes.full: Thutmose III, taking the narrow pass of Aruna against his officers' advice, surprised a coalition of Canaanite cities led by the prince of Kadesh at Megiddo in about 1457 BC, and defeated them in a battle in which the enemy fled into the city; after a seven-month siege the city fell and its booty is listed at Karnak, the earliest battle in history for which we have a detailed account.
nodes.src: Thutmose III, Annals; Redford 2003; Eric Cline, The Battles of Armageddon (2000).

nodes.label: One-Year War
nodes.full: The Hittite king Suppiluliuma I crossed the Euphrates and captured Washukanni in his first Syrian war, then made vassals of Ugarit, Nuhashshe, Amurru and Qatna, and took Carchemish; the Hittite sources speak of a one-year war of conquest of the Mitannian west, and the Egyptian vassals in Syria lost their protector.
nodes.src: Deeds of Suppiluliuma; Bryce 1998; Singer.

nodes.label: Qadesh
nodes.full: Ramesses II marched with four divisions to Qadesh in his fifth year and was surprised by Muwatalli II's army of some 3,500 chariots and tens of thousands of infantry, which attacked the Re division as it marched; Ramesses held his ground with his bodyguard until the Ne'arin troops arrived, and the battle ended with no clear winner; Ramesses recorded a victory in the poem and bulletin on the walls of Abu Simbel and the Ramesseum, while the Hittites kept Qadesh.
nodes.src: Qadesh Poem and Bulletin (Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions vol. 2); Hittite sources; Mark Healy, Qadesh 1300 BC (1993); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Nihriya
nodes.full: Tukulti-Ninurta I of Assyria, who had taken land in the north held by Hatti, defeated the army of the Hittite king Tudhaliya IV at Nihriya in the upper Tigris region in the 1230s and took 28,800 Hittites and their auxiliaries as captives; the Hittite king's letters speak of the Assyrian king in terms of a rival and the victory made Assyria the greatest military power of the east.
nodes.src: Tukulti-Ninurta Epic; Grayson, Assyrian Royal Inscriptions vol. 1; Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Assyrian capture of Babylon
nodes.full: Tukulti-Ninurta I defeated the Kassite king Kashtiliash IV, took him in chains and entered Babylon about 1225 BC, tearing down the city's walls and removing the statue of Marduk to Assur; he ruled Babylonia directly for seven years, the first Assyrian to do so, until he was killed by his own sons in a revolt in about 1208 BC.
nodes.src: Tukulti-Ninurta Epic; Babylonian Chronicle P; Grayson 1972; Van De Mieroop 2016.

nodes.label: Struggle for Amurru
nodes.full: Amurru, in the Syrian coast, changed sides between Egypt and Hatti, notably under Aziru in the Amarna age and Benteshina and Shapili later; Seti I recovered Qadesh in 1290 BC and Muwatalli took it back, and the border zone was the object of the competition that led to Qadesh.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters EA 156–161; Kitchen 1982; Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Treaty of Qadesh
nodes.full: In the twenty-first year of Ramesses II the Egyptian and Hittite kings, Ramesses and Hattusili III, made a treaty of peace and alliance and mutual extradition, of which both versions survive, the Egyptian in hieroglyphs on the walls of Karnak and the Ramesseum and the Hittite in cuneiform on clay tablets from Hattusa; a copy of the silver tablet is displayed at the United Nations in New York as the oldest known peace treaty.
nodes.src: Treaty of Qadesh (Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions vol. 2; Beckman, Hittite Diplomatic Texts, 1996); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Amarna letters
nodes.full: The archive of the Egyptian foreign office at Akhetaten, found in 1887, holds some 380 clay tablets in Akkadian, the diplomatic language of the age, from the Great Kings of Babylonia, Mitanni, Hatti, Assyria and Alashiya and the Syrian and Canaanite vassals, with complaints about gifts, marriages and rank; the rulers address each other as brothers and the system was that of an ordered society of equals.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters (trans. Moran 1992); Amanda Podany, Brotherhood of Kings (2010); Raymond Cohen and Raymond Westbrook (eds.), Amarna Diplomacy (2000).

nodes.label: Hittite Laws
nodes.full: The Hittite Laws, in two tablets of some 200 clauses, written in Hittite from about 1650 and revised in the following centuries, deal with homicide, theft, marriage, land and service, and prescribe compensation in most cases rather than the death penalty; they show a society of free men and slaves and of tenures tied to service, the luzzi.
nodes.src: Hittite Laws (trans. Harry Hoffner, 1997); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Egyptian administration in Canaan
nodes.full: Egypt ruled Canaan through three provinces with seats at Gaza, Kumidi and Sumur, and Egyptian commissioners, with garrisons, granaries and temples, collected tribute and ran the tribute and supply of the army; the vassal kings were left in office, their sons were taken to Egypt for education and the system worked by threat, gifts and the fear of the army.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters EA 288, 296; Na'aman 2005; Carolyn Higginbotham, Egyptianization and Elite Emulation in Ramesside Palestine (2000).

nodes.label: Kassite kudurrus
nodes.full: The Kassite kings recorded gifts of land to officers, temples and favourites on boundary stones, kudurrus, carved with the symbols of the gods that would punish anyone who moved or erased them; the stones are the best record of the land holding of Babylonia and the gods of the Kassite and Babylonian pantheon.
nodes.src: Kudurru texts (Slanski, The Babylonian Entitlement narûs (kudurrus), 2003); Brinkman 1968.

nodes.label: The Aten
nodes.full: Akhenaten, in about his fifth year, proclaimed the Aten, the sun's disc, the only god of Egypt, closed or neglected the temples of Amun and the others and ordered that the names of the other gods be erased; the Great Hymn to the Aten, preserved in the tombs of Amarna, praises the sun's life-giving rays on all peoples, and after his death the old cults were restored under Tutankhamun and the Aten was proscribed.
nodes.src: Great Hymn to the Aten (tomb of Ay at Amarna); Jan Assmann, Moses the Egyptian (1997); Erik Hornung, Akhenaten and the Religion of Light (1999).

nodes.label: Thousand gods of Hatti
nodes.full: The Hittite state religion, under the king as chief priest, combined the Hattic storm god and sun goddess of Arinna with Hurrian and Luwian gods, and in the treaty texts the gods of every vassal were invoked as witnesses, making up the thousand gods of Hatti; the open-air sanctuary at Yazılıkaya, with its rock-cut reliefs of a procession of twelve gods and the king's god Sarruma, is the best monument.
nodes.src: Hittite treaties; Yazılıkaya reliefs; Volkert Haas, Geschichte der hethitischen Religion (1994); Bryce 2005.

nodes.label: Baal Cycle
nodes.full: The Baal Cycle on clay tablets from the library of the high priest at Ugarit tells of the storm god Baal's battles with the sea god Yam and the death god Mot and of the building of his palace on Mount Sapan, in poetry whose phrases appear in the Hebrew psalms; the El and Asherah, Anat and Shapshu of the pantheon were known later in Canaan.
nodes.src: Ugaritic Baal Cycle (KTU 1.1–1.6); Mark Smith, The Ugaritic Baal Cycle (1994); Smith, The Early History of God (2002).

nodes.label: Karnak
nodes.full: The temple of Amun at Karnak grew under the New Kingdom pharaohs into the largest religious complex of the ancient world, with the pylons of Thutmose I and III, Hatshepsut's obelisks and the great hypostyle hall of Seti I and Ramesses II, and its priesthood held a large part of Egypt's land and gold; the priests of Amun were the chief rivals of the throne in the Amarna period.
nodes.src: Karnak inscriptions; Peter Brand and Betsy Bryan; Donald Redford, Akhenaten: The Heretic King (1984).

nodes.label: the art of the Amarna court
nodes.full: The sculptors and painters of Akhenaten's reign broke with the conventions of earlier art and showed the royal family with elongated heads, thick thighs and drooping bellies, in scenes of intimacy with the children under the sun's rays; the bust of Nefertiti found by Ludwig Borchardt in 1912 in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose, in Berlin, is the best-known work.
nodes.src: Nefertiti bust (Berlin, Neues Museum, ÄM 21300); Kemp 2012; Cyril Aldred, Akhenaten and Nefertiti (1973).

nodes.label: Hattusa
nodes.full: The walls of Hattusa, with their Lion Gate, Sphinx Gate and the King's Gate with its relief of a warrior god, enclose some 180 hectares, with the great temple, the royal citadel Büyükkale and some thirty temples; the poterns, the Yerkapı rampart with its tunnel and the rock-cut relief of Tudhaliya IV at Yazılıkaya show Hittite monumental art.
nodes.src: Hattusa excavations (Neve; Seeher, Hattusha Guide, 2006); Bryce 2005.

nodes.label: Archive of Ugarit
nodes.full: The Ras Shamra excavations from 1929 uncovered in the royal palace and the houses of officials several thousand tablets in Sumerian, Akkadian, Hurrian, Hittite, Egyptian and Ugaritic, which record legal and economic documents, diplomacy, rituals and myths; the library of the high priest, the house of Rapanu and the house of Urtenu held literature and scholarly lists in several languages.
nodes.src: Ugaritic archives (RS tablets); Yon 2006; Daniel Pardee.

nodes.label: Abu Simbel and the Ramesseum
nodes.full: Ramesses II's rock temples at Abu Simbel in Nubia, with four colossal seated figures 20 metres high on its facade and a smaller temple of Nefertari, were carved in about 1264–1244 BC and moved in 1964–1968 to save them from the Aswan Dam's lake; the Ramesseum at Thebes bears the Qadesh reliefs and the toppled colossus of the king that inspired Shelley's Ozymandias.
nodes.src: Kitchen 1982; UNESCO Nubian campaign (1960–1968); Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions.

nodes.label: Language of diplomacy
nodes.full: Akkadian cuneiform on clay was used as the common language of diplomacy by Egypt, Hatti, Mitanni, Alashiya and the vassal cities, with scribal schools that taught Sumerian and Akkadian lists and literature at Hattusa, Ugarit, Emar, Amarna and Megiddo; the standard text of the Gilgamesh epic was produced in this period, and Hittite and Hurrian versions were found in Anatolia.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters; Hittite archives; Andrew George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic (2003); Podany 2010.

nodes.label: The alphabet
nodes.full: The scribes at Ugarit devised a cuneiform alphabet of 30 signs for writing their own language in the fourteenth century BC, with an abecedary of the order which survives as the basis of the Phoenician and Hebrew alphabets, while workers in the Sinai turquoise mines and in Egypt developed a linear alphabetic script for a Semitic language which was the ancestor of the Phoenician; the invention opened writing to a larger number of people.
nodes.src: Ugaritic abecedaries (KTU 5.6); Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions; Joseph Naveh, Early History of the Alphabet (1982); Orly Goldwasser (2010).

nodes.label: Hittite scribes
nodes.full: The Hittite scribes wrote annals, treaties, laws, prayers, rituals, oracles, myths of Hattic, Hurrian and Mesopotamian origin and the first known Indo-European texts, in a language deciphered by Bedřich Hrozný in 1915; the archives of Hattusa hold some 30,000 tablets, and the ritual and festival texts give the best record of Anatolian religion.
nodes.src: Bedřich Hrozný, Die Sprache der Hethiter (1917); Hoffner and Melchert, A Grammar of the Hittite Language (2008); Bryce 2005.

nodes.label: Gift exchange
nodes.full: The Amarna letters list the gifts of gold, lapis lazuli, horses, chariots, ebony, perfumes, textiles, ivory and women sent by the kings to each other, with Egyptian gold the object of constant requests ("gold in your land is like dirt"); the exchange of goods at a ritual of friendship is a form of trade at the state level in a time when no market ruled prices.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters EA 7, 14, 16, 27; Liverani, International Relations in the Ancient Near East (2001); Podany 2010.

nodes.label: Uluburun
nodes.full: A ship sunk off the southern Turkish coast about 1320 BC and excavated by George Bass and Cemal Pulak in 1984–1994 carried ten tons of copper ingots from Cyprus, a ton of tin, glass ingots, Canaanite jars with terebinth resin, ivory, ebony, gold and silver jewellery, Mycenaean pottery and a gold scarab of Nefertiti, the best view of the trade between the powers and the Aegean.
nodes.src: Cemal Pulak, ‘The Uluburun Shipwreck’ (1998); George Bass, ‘A Bronze Age Shipwreck at Ulu Burun’, American Journal of Archaeology 90 (1986); Cline, 1177 BC (2014).

nodes.label: Palace economies
nodes.full: The kingdoms' economies were run by palaces with their own estates, workshops, scribes and flocks, which collected, stored and redistributed the produce of villages, as the Ugarit and Linear B tablets show, in lists of rations, textiles and metals; trade was carried on by royal agents and merchants, such as the tamkarum of Ugarit, who traded with the king's capital and sometimes on their own account.
nodes.src: Ugarit archive; Linear B tablets of Pylos; Michael Heltzer, The Internal Organization of the Kingdom of Ugarit (1982); Van De Mieroop 2016.

nodes.label: Copper of Alashiya
nodes.full: Alashiya, probably Cyprus, ruled by a king who wrote to the pharaoh as a brother, was the main supplier of copper in the Mediterranean, sending in the Amarna letters 500 and 200 talents of copper in gifts; the city of Enkomi with its workshops, scripts and fortifications was a trading town, and the Cypriot Linear script was used.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters EA 33–40; Enkomi excavations; Cline 2014.

nodes.label: Chariot and Kikkuli
nodes.full: The light two-horse chariot with spoked wheels came to dominate the armies of the powers in the second millennium; the Mitannian horse trainer Kikkuli wrote in Hittite about 1400 BC a manual of 184 days of training for chariot horses, with Indo-Aryan loan words for numbers, on four tablets from Hattusa.
nodes.src: Kikkuli text (Starke, 1995); Mary Littauer and Joost Crouwel, Wheeled Vehicles and Ridden Animals in the Ancient Near East (1979); Bryce 2005.

nodes.label: Glass and faience
nodes.full: Glassmaking, first in Mesopotamia and Egypt about 1500 BC, produced opaque coloured glass vessels formed on a sand core and ingots such as those on the Uluburun ship, as the workshops of Amarna and Nuzi show; the Egyptian court's rich blue glass and faience were exported over the Mediterranean.
nodes.src: Julian Henderson, The Science and Archaeology of Materials (2000); Paul Nicholson, Egyptian Faience and Glass (1993); Pulak 1998.

nodes.label: Iron and fortification
nodes.full: Iron objects were rare and precious in the age, as a gift of an iron dagger or an iron bracelet sent by Hittite kings shows, and bronze remained the main metal; at the same time cities of the Levant and Anatolia were strengthened with casemate and glacis walls, while the fortresses of Egypt's northern road and of Hattusa's city walls are the main defensive works.
nodes.src: Bryce 2005; Jane Waldbaum, From Bronze to Iron (1978).

nodes.label: Diplomatic marriages
nodes.full: Amenhotep III married Mitannian princesses, Gilukhepa and Tadukhepa, and a Babylonian princess, and refused to give an Egyptian princess in return, as Kadashman-Enlil complained; Ramesses II married a daughter of Hattusili III about 1245 and a second later and the Hittite queen Puduhepa and the Egyptian queen Nefertari exchanged letters and gifts.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters EA 1, 4, 29; Hattusili III–Ramesses correspondence (Edel, 1994); Podany 2010.

nodes.label: Ahhiyawa and Mycenaeans
nodes.full: Hittite texts speak of a kingdom of Ahhiyawa across the sea, which held Millawanda (Miletus) in western Anatolia and was treated by Hattusili III and Tudhaliya IV as a Great King's equal, though in the end excluded from the list; most scholars identify Ahhiyawa with the Mycenaean Greeks, and the Mycenaean ceramics at Ugarit, Amarna and Uluburun show their trade.
nodes.src: Tawagalawa Letter; Millawata Letter; Trevor Bryce, The Trojans and Their Neighbours (2006); Cline 2014.

nodes.label: Nubian gold
nodes.full: Egypt held Nubia as far as Napata, the viceroy of Kush governed it with garrisons and temples, and sent the gold of the eastern desert and Nubia, which gave Egypt the reputation of a land where gold was like dust; Nubian chiefs' sons were raised at the court and the supply of gold to the pharaoh was the means of his diplomacy with the other Great Kings.
nodes.src: Viceroy Huy's tomb (TT 40); Amarna Letters EA 16, 19; László Török, The Kingdom of Kush (1997).

nodes.label: Plague of Suppiluliuma
nodes.full: Prisoners brought from Egypt after the Syrian war brought a plague that spread over Hatti, killed Suppiluliuma I and his heir Arnuwanda II and ravaged the country for twenty years, as Mursili II's Plague Prayers describe, with an appeal to the gods to end the pestilence which he saw as a punishment for a broken treaty with Egypt.
nodes.src: Plague Prayers of Mursili II (trans. Singer, 2002); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Drought
nodes.full: Pollen records from lakes in Syria and Cyprus and speleothem and sediment evidence suggest a period of increasing aridity from about 1250 BC, and Hittite and Ugaritic texts of the age speak of famines and ask the Egyptian pharaoh for grain, as in a letter from Hattusili III and a Merneptah inscription that records grain sent to Hatti; the role of drought in the collapse of the system is much debated.
nodes.src: David Kaniewski et al., ‘Environmental Roots of the Late Bronze Age Crisis’, PLoS ONE 8 (2013); Eric Cline 2014; Merneptah's Karnak inscription.

nodes.label: Thera eruption
nodes.full: The volcanic eruption of Thera on Santorini, one of the largest of the Holocene, buried the town of Akrotiri under pumice and left ash on Crete and over the eastern Mediterranean; its date, about 1620–1600 BC on radiocarbon and tree rings and about 1550 on Egyptian synchronisations, is disputed, and its effects on the Minoan palaces, and on the Egyptian traditions of darkness, remain uncertain.
nodes.src: Walter Friedrich, Fire in the Sea (2000); Sturt Manning, A Test of Time (1999); Cline 2014.

nodes.label: Puduhepa
nodes.full: Puduhepa, a priest's daughter from Kizzuwatna in Cilicia, married Hattusili III and acted as co-ruler with her own seal, corresponded with Ramesses II, Nefertari and the Kassite king, took part in the legal proceedings of the empire and revised the cult of the gods; her prayers and letters are among the most personal documents of Hittite literature.
nodes.src: Puduhepa letters (Edel 1994); Hittite prayers; Singer 2002; Bryce 2005.

nodes.label: Tiye and Nefertiti
nodes.full: Queen Tiye, the principal wife of Amenhotep III, who corresponded with Tushratta and appeared with the king in statuary and was given a temple in Nubia, and Nefertiti, Akhenaten's queen, shown in the reliefs of Amarna at the king's side, smiting enemies and driving a chariot, and possibly briefly ruling as a king, are the best-known royal women of the New Kingdom.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters EA 26; Kozloff 2012; Dodson 2009; Joyce Tyldesley, Nefertiti (1998).

nodes.label: Habiru
nodes.full: The habiru (Apiru), landless groups of displaced people, mercenaries, brigands and servants named in texts from Mesopotamia, Syria, Anatolia and Egypt, were used by city-state kings in their wars and accused in the Amarna letters of seizing towns; whether they were a social class or an ethnic group, and what relation they bore to the Hebrews, has been much argued.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters EA 67–90, 286–289; Na'aman 1986; Moran 1992.

nodes.label: Scribes and merchants of Ugarit
nodes.full: The scribes of Ugarit, among them Ilimilku, who wrote the Baal Cycle in the reign of king Niqmaddu, trained in the royal school and held posts in the palace; the merchants (tamkaru) and ship-owners of Ugarit traded in tin, copper, wine, oil and cloth with Egypt, Cyprus and Anatolia, and the sailors' families are named in lists of the palace.
nodes.src: Ugarit tablets (KTU 1.1–1.6); Yon 2006; Heltzer 1982.

nodes.label: The Hittite sack of Babylon and the end of the Middle Bronze Age
nodes.full: The Hittite raid on Babylon in about 1595 BC ended Hammurabi’s dynasty and left Babylonia to the Kassites, as the Egyptian New Kingdom and Mitanni rose from the ruins of the Hyksos and Amorite states.
nodes.src: background — see the Babylon 2004–1595 BC folio (babylon-2004bc-1595bc)

nodes.label: The collapse of the system
nodes.full: The destructions of Ugarit, Hattusa and many of the Mycenaean palaces about 1200–1180 BC, with the Sea Peoples’ raids on Egypt, ended the Late Bronze Age order.
nodes.src: background — see the Egypt 1200–664 BC and Philistia folios (egypt-1200bc-664bc)
